prompt.context: Our client is a large national health care payer (health insurance company, think Aetna) exploring the launch of a new disease management ("DM") program to better serve its 5 million members. The idea is to hire and train a team of "Health Coaches" to specialize in a single disease area (e.g., heart disease, diabetes, etc). Each Coach will manage a portfolio of patients to reduce the costs of overall health expenditures (e.g., reminders to take drugs, provide limited medical advice, suggested diet, etc). Studies show that once a month contact with each patient reduces health spending by 5%, on average.
prompt.question: Should our client launch the program? If so, what steps should it take?

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: With spiraling health care costs, the industry is under pressure to innovate. Assume client is first to market. Past attempts to purely automate DM have yielded minimal savings.

All activity is conducted remotely via phone/email. Typical profile is a registered nurse that wants to work from home. It is difficult to actually reach patients, so Coaches can contact 8 members per day (assume 25 days per month).

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to employ a Health Coach?
clarifying_info.a: Annual costs per Coach: $60K salary + 20% other (training, benefits, laptop, etc). There are no other program costs.

clarifying_info.q: What types of members does the client have?
clarifying_info.a: Members are segmented into Group (employer-sponsored plans), Individual (non-group, e.g., private contractors), and 65+ (Medicare Advantage, premiums funded by government). Exhibit 1 shows the full segmentation.

clarifying_info.q: What disease areas should we consider?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to specialize each Coach in a single disease area. Exhibit 1 shows the breakdown of health conditions across segments.

exhibits.title: Client's member segmentation by health condition
exhibits.shows: A chart breaking down the client's 5 million members by segment (Group, Individual, 65+) and by health condition (e.g., diabetic, heart disease, other). Shows what percentage of each segment has each condition.
exhibits.data: 65+ segment = 20% of total members (1M); 40% of 65+ members are diabetic. Group and Individual segments also shown with respective diabetic and other condition percentages.

exhibits.title: Average cost data (Per Member Per Month)
exhibits.shows: A table listing average Per Member Per Month (PMPM) medical costs by segment, and a multiplier showing how much more diabetic members cost relative to the segment average.
exhibits.data: Individual: avg PMPM $150, diabetic factor 4x; Group: avg PMPM $100, diabetic factor 4x; 65+: avg PMPM $300, diabetic factor 4x

framework: Program Savings: identify which customer segment and disease area drives the greatest per-member costs and would benefit most from the DM program (customer segmentation by disease area and cost per member)
Program Costs: calculate cost per Health Coach (salary + other) and determine portfolio size / capacity (members per coach)
Profitability / Break-even: determine whether savings from reduced health spending exceed the cost of deploying Health Coaches, by segment
Risks: assess whether key assumptions hold (5% savings, contact rate), competitive response, and regulatory / liability considerations

questions.prompt: Which member segment and disease area should the client focus on first, and why?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates should segment members by sickness level: 65+ (Medicare) patients are the sickest and highest-cost, followed by Individual, then Group (youngest, healthiest). Within segments, diabetics make up the largest portion of high-cost members and, as a chronic behavioral disease (Type 2), are most likely to benefit from coaching. Therefore the client should focus on 65+ diabetics first. Candidates should note that sicker = higher baseline spend = larger absolute dollar savings from the 5% reduction.

questions.prompt: How many 65+ diabetic members does the client have?
questions.guidance: Use Exhibit 1 to read off segment share and diabetic proportion, then multiply by total membership.

math.setup: Total members x 65+ segment % x diabetic % within 65+

questions.prompt: What is the maximum portfolio size (patients per Health Coach)?
questions.guidance: Use the contact rate and working days to compute how many unique patients a coach can contact once per month.

math.setup: Contacts per day x working days per month = max portfolio size
steps: Each patient requires once-a-month contact, so max portfolio = 200 patients per Coach

questions.prompt: What is the annual cost per Health Coach?
What are the annual savings generated by one Health Coach managing a full portfolio of 65+ diabetics?
questions.guidance: Savings per patient per month = avg PMPM for 65+ x diabetic factor x 5% savings rate. Annualize and multiply by portfolio size.

math.setup: Avg PMPM (65+) x diabetic factor x 5% savings x 12 months x portfolio size
steps: $300 (65+ avg PMPM) x 4 (diabetic factor) = $1,200 PMPM per diabetic member
$1,200 x 5% = $60 savings per member per month
$60 x 12 months = $720 savings per member per year
$720 x 200 patients = $144,000 savings per Coach per year

questions.prompt: Is the Health Coach program profitable for the 65+ diabetic segment? What is the profit per Coach, and total profit if all 65+ diabetics are coached?
questions.guidance: Compare savings to cost per Coach, then scale to the total number of Coaches needed.

math.setup: Profit per Coach = Savings per Coach - Cost per Coach; Total Coaches needed = 65+ diabetics / portfolio size; Total profit = profit per Coach x total Coaches
steps: Profit per Coach = $144,000 - $72,000 = $72,000 (a 2x return on cost)
math.answer: $72,000 profit per Coach per year; $144M total annual profit for the 65+ diabetic segment

questions.prompt: Is the program profitable for the Individual and Group diabetic segments?
questions.guidance: Use the respective PMPM figures from Exhibit 2. Individual PMPM is $150 (diabetic 4x = $600), Group is $100 (diabetic 4x = $400). Apply same 5% savings and $72K cost.

math.setup: Same formula: Avg PMPM x 4 x 5% x 12 x 200 vs. $72K cost
steps: Individual: $150 x 4 = $600; $600 x 5% = $30/month; $30 x 12 x 200 = $72,000 savings — exactly breaks even
Group: $100 x 4 = $400; $400 x 5% = $20/month; $20 x 12 x 200 = $48,000 savings vs. $72,000 cost — a loss of $24,000 per Coach
math.answer: Individual segment breaks even ($72K savings = $72K cost); Group segment is unprofitable ($48K savings vs. $72K cost, loss of $24K per Coach)

brainstorming.prompt: There are 650K Group diabetics left uncoached and the segment is currently unprofitable. What ideas do you have to make the Group segment profitable or find value from it?

categories.name: Reduce program costs
ideas: More efficient DM delivery (e.g., bi-monthly contact instead of monthly)
Group coaching sessions at employers (higher contact efficiency)

categories.name: Increase revenue / savings
ideas: Target Group members most likely to respond with savings well above 5% average
Charge employers a fee for the Health Coach service (employers benefit from healthier workforce)
Bundle with other wellness services employers already pay for

categories.name: Alternative program designs
ideas: Automate low-risk touchpoints, reserve human coaches for highest-cost members only
Partner with employers to provide on-site coaching (lower contact difficulty)
Leverage technology (apps, wearables) to lower cost per contact

recommendation: The client should launch the Health Coach program, focusing first on Type 2 diabetics in the 65+ Medicare segment
The 65+ diabetic segment yields $72K profit per Coach and $144M total annual profit across 2,000 Coaches — a 2x return on investment
The Individual segment breaks even and should be considered for launch based on customer retention and ethical rationale
The Group segment is currently unprofitable and should not be launched without program redesign
risks: The 5% average cost reduction assumption may not hold across all patients — a pilot is needed to validate
Coach contact rates (8/day, 200/month portfolio) are an assumption; actual reachability may be lower
Competitive response: if competitors launch similar programs, savings advantage may erode
Regulatory and liability risks associated with Coaches providing medical advice remotely
Adverse selection risk if marketing the program externally attracts the highest-cost members
next_steps: Launch a pilot program to validate key assumptions (5% savings rate, Coach capacity, patient reachability)
If pilot confirms assumptions, expand to the full 65+ diabetic segment (2,000 Coaches, $144M annual profit)
Evaluate the Individual segment for launch despite break-even economics (retention, brand, moral rationale)
Redesign the Group program to improve unit economics before broader rollout
Explore selling Health Coach services to other payers as a revenue opportunity, subject to regulatory and data-sharing review
